sources.headline: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
sources.text: US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries."Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course"."The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

sources.headline: Ukrainian MP calls U.S.-Russia diesel deal a 'betrayal'
sources.text:
NPR's Joel Rose speaks with Ukrainian Minister of Parliament, Oleksandr Merezhko, about the U.S.'s diesel deal with Russia will impact Ukraine.
Transcript
JOEL ROSE, HOST: President Trump and President Zelenskyy of Ukraine have had a stormy relationship, and this weekend, it's taken another chaotic turn. On Friday, Trump announced an agreement with Russia's President Putin to ease sanctions and reopen flows of diesel fuel. That did not go over well in Kyiv. Zelenskyy called Trump, quote, "weak," unquote. Trump responded yesterday saying Ukraine should get a new president.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does.ROSE: Then today, Zelenskyy offered to hold new elections, but only if there is a ceasefire, as he told ABC's "This Week."(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "THIS WEEK")PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off - total ceasefire, 60 days - and we will organize elections.ROSE: Shortly afterward, President Trump posted on Truth Social that both parties have agreed to an energy ceasefire. But Zelenskyy told media outlets that was news to him. This geopolitical tussling matters. The war between Ukraine and Russia is in its fourth year. U.S. military and financial aid to Ukraine hangs in the balance, and the fighting has exacerbated a global energy crisis.To understand the view from Kyiv tonight, we called Oleksandr Merezhko. He's a member of Ukraine's Parliament and the chairman of its committee on foreign policy. I asked him if he knows anything about a ceasefire.OLEKSANDR MEREZHKO: First of all, there is absolutely no ceasefire because right now, I'm sitting in a dark apartment when there is no power, when there is no water. In the morning, there were nonstop air-raid alerts going off. Then I heard loud - rather loud explosions. So we don't have any ceasefire or energy truce whatsoever. And to me, this statement by President Trump came as a quite surprise.ROSE: What do you think is going on? I mean, he says both parties have agreed.MEREZHKO: First of all, our President Volodymyr Zelenskyy - he didn't confirm that there is any ceasefire. But I'm afraid that it's part of internal American politics on the eve of the midterm elections. And maybe President Trump - well, actually, it's his typical political style, maybe, to make such statements which later are not confirmed.ROSE: Diplomatically speaking, are things as bad as they look?MEREZHKO: Well, first of all, the good news about all the story is that American Congress - most of them are on the side of Ukraine. The situation is not that bad. Of course, there might be some disagreements between President Trump and President Zelenskyy, but it's a normal thing. So I think it's part of normal diplomatic or political process.ROSE: What is the state of Ukrainian infrastructure? And what is your incentive to try to stop attacks from Russia on that infrastructure right now?MEREZHKO: Our critical infrastructure is being hit practically each day, and it's not in the best shape. But at the same time, the thing is that ahead of us is a very difficult winter and Putin will definitely weaponize. This winter, he wants to continue to destroy us. He wants to create humanitarian catastrophe. We're trying to prepare our power grid for that. But of course, we understand that the coming winter will be very difficult.ROSE: What has been the reaction in Ukraine today to these latest developments?MEREZHKO: We were outraged, honestly speaking, by this so-called diesel deal between President Trump and Putin because, yes, it's taken as a betrayal because we don't understand what's going on. Putin is conducting a crime of genocide against Ukrainian people. And if our closest friend, the United States, is giving some support or giving money to Russian war machine, it's tantamount to helping Putin to kill us.ROSE: As you know, the midterm elections here in the U.S. are looming, and President Trump wants diesel supplies for Americans urgently, and he has blamed Ukraine, in part, for the high diesel prices that U.S. farmers and truckers are facing. How do you respond to that?MEREZHKO: We wouldn't like Ukraine to become a hostage to internal political struggle in the United States. And we understand that situation before the midterm elections is getting tense, but Ukraine cannot be blamed. I believe it's very unfair and even immoral to blame the victim of the aggression. We're trying to protect ourselves. We're trying to destroy Russian war machine, which is killing us. And the only way to do it is to deprive Russia of oil revenues and its capabilities, including oil refineries. So - and I believe that the United States - it should support, not blame the victim. To me, it's deeply immoral.ROSE: I've been speaking to Oleksandr Merezhko. He is a member of Ukraine's Parliament and the chairman of its committee on foreign policy. Thank you very much for joining us.MEREZHKO: Thank you.

China is likely to view the latest US dealings with Russia as “transactional”, according to observers, who said Beijing was likely to wait and see what the longer-term impact would be given the possibility that Donald Trump might abruptly change course again.

The US president announced that under a deal with Vladimir Putin, Russia would “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets.

He wrote on social media that another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, with a further 1 million tonnes “within a short period of time”.

sources.headline: 'America first': Trump defends Russia diesel deal amid bipartisan backlash
sources.text: Trump described the arrangement as a 'big deal' and thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for agreeing to supply what he called "massive amounts" of diesel.US President Donald Trump on Monday defended his decision to allow Russian diesel supplies to the United States, saying his administration had acted in the interests of the American people. He also accused the media of ignoring the European Union's energy payments to Moscow, as Ukraine criticised the deal and the EU announced fresh sanctions against Russia.In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump claimed that the European Union had paid Russia $250 billion for energy and accused the media of avoiding the issue."The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn’t want to get near that story," Trump wrote.Defending his energy policy, he added, "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!"The remarks come amid criticism of the proposed Russian diesel supplies, which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has argued could help Moscow finance its war against Ukraine.Zelenskyy criticises deal as EU announces fresh sanctionsZelenskyy welcomed the European Union's latest sanctions against Russia, describing them as the "right and necessary signal" towards ending the conflict. He thanked European Council President António Costa, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU member states for adopting the measures.The European Council said the new package targets 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial network. These include 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals serving as their chief executive officers.The latest measures bring the total number of individuals and entities listed under the EU sanctions regime supporting Ukraine's territorial integrity to nearly 4,600.The sanctions focus on mid-level suppliers that play a key role in Russia's military-industrial network. These companies collectively generate an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros and employ more than 250,000 people, according to the European Council.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said sustained economic pressure on Moscow was necessary to end the war. The latest sanctions also target individuals linked to elections held in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.Zelenskyy linked the sanctions to renewed Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. He said the strikes came a day after Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, claiming both sides had agreed to it."It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities. Just today, the Russians attacked six energy facilities in Ukraine. Across the country, 33 people were injured. This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of increasing revenues for its war machine," Zelenskyy said.The Ukrainian president has argued that the proposed diesel deal could increase Moscow's revenues and strengthen its ability to continue the war, which has lasted more than four years.Trump announces large Russian diesel suppliesTrump announced the proposed diesel deal on Friday in a post on Truth Social. He said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the United States, followed by another 500,000 tonnes during November.He added that a further one million tonnes would be supplied immediately afterwards, with another three million tonnes expected within a short period, depending on the condition of Russia's diesel refineries.Trump described the arrangement as a "big deal" and thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for agreeing to supply what he called "massive amounts" of diesel."I think you heard about the oil deal with Russia. That is a big deal. That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country. I want to thank President Putin. We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it is diesel, which is what we want," Trump told reporters outside the White House before leaving for Syracuse, New York, for the midterm election campaign.Putin says Russian supplies could benefit global economyPutin has also defended the proposed energy supplies, saying they could benefit the global economy.According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the Russian president made the remarks following a telephone conversation with Trump on Friday. The two leaders discussed Ukraine and Iran, as well as the global energy situation."In discussing the global energy situation, Russia reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets. I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy," Putin said.The proposed deal has highlighted the contrasting approaches of Washington and Brussels towards Russian energy supplies. While Trump has defended the arrangement on the grounds of American interests, the EU has continued to tighten economic pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.

sources.headline: Russia says its diesel exports may exceed volumes announced by Trump
sources.text: MOSCOW - Russia, which has seen diesel exports collapse due to Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and self-imposed overseas sales restrictions, will be able to return them near former levels and above amounts US President Donald Trump has outlined, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct 12.Trump announced on Oct 9 that Russia had agreed to supply ​diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its ‌war on Ukraine.“We will see how the situation develops further, but Russia has the capacity to increase diesel fuel exports,” Novak, President Vladimir Putin’s pointman on oil, said on Rossiya-24 state TV channel.“By the end of the year, exports could reach 3.0-3.5 million metric tonnes per month, returning to the levels seen before the crisis,” he said.Before Ukraine launched a barrage of drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in 2024-2025, Russian diesel exports amounted to more than 3 million metric tonnes per month.Despite a self-imposed export ban, Moscow has continued to supply diesel to countries, mostly in Central Asia, under government deals. Russian diesel exports to Central Asia in September amounted to 427,000 tonnes, according to industry sources.Soaring US diesel prices are hurting US truckers and farmers, and are a concern for voters and political parties ahead of US midterm elections on Nov 3.Novak also said that under the deal with Trump, Russian diesel supplies will partially balance global supply and demand.“We are already seeing this effect, including in global diesel markets, where prices have fallen by around 5-6%,” Novak said.Trump said on Oct 9 that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets.That is less than a day’s supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels per day.Trump also said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. REUTERS

sources.headline: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
sources.text: Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration.Trump rewards Putin and betrays Ukraine with Russia diesel deal - The Latest“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted.However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections.Graph showing increase in price of US dieselUS prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon, according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday.Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small.“They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.”The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.”However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe.The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products.Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader”.On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output.“The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

sources.headline: Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
sources.text: United States Senator Thom Tillis has questioned the legality of President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily relax sanctions on Russian diesel, in an effort to bring down record-high fuel prices caused by the US-Israel war against Iran.During a Sunday interview on the NBC News television show Meet the Press, Tillis argued that the sanctions relief could violate congressional law.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Zelenskyy says Russia violated energy truce announced by Trumplist 2 of 3Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy tieslist 3 of 3Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia dealend of list“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” said Tillis.Trump’s decision has unsettled some Republican lawmakers who continue to support Ukraine in its war with Russia, which began in February 2022, after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of the eastern European country.Tillis warned that his vote in support of Trump’s legislative priorities would be contingent on the White House reversing course.“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” Tillis said.Tillis has become a critical voice within the Republican Party, denouncing what he sees as overreach from the Trump administration.But his time as a senator is nearly at a close. In June 2025, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in the November 3 midterm elections, after Trump threatened him with a primary challenge in his home state of North Carolina. His term ends in January.Separately on Sunday, Tillis joined a bipartisan group of senators in issuing a letter to denounce the sanctions relief for Russia.The group included Republicans like Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Curtis of Utah, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal.“The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” the senators wrote.Another retiring Republican lawmaker, Representative Don Bacon, also said on Friday that “propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities”.The pushback points to schisms within the Republican Party over Russia’s invasion.Figures from the party’s establishment wing have generally pressed for robust support for Kyiv, while other party members have been sceptical of continued US support for Ukraine.Trump himself has been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusing the government in Kyiv of impeding a US-negotiated ceasefire.“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does,” Trump said on Saturday. “That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”A day earlier, Trump had announced that a call with Putin had concluded with an agreement to provide 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the global marketplace, with a further 500,000 tonnes to be delivered in November.In an interview with Fox and Friends on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the administration’s decision to ease some sanctions on Moscow was necessary to obtain relief from surging diesel prices.“We’re going to do it with all the legal authorities we have,” Bessent said.Analysts have said that the decision is unlikely to bring prices down in the long term. Critics like Tillis have also pointed to previous law barring the importation of Russian fuel, including a 2022 executive order.A law signed last month — named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — also prohibits US investment in the Russian energy sector.This year’s rise in global fuel prices has largely been attributed to the US-Israel war against Iran, which began in February. As a result of that war, Iran has limited commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the fuel trade.Tillis pointed to those circumstances in his remarks to Meet the Press.“ If President Trump wants to end the strain on energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran, and number two, recognise that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war,” Tillis said.“It’s Vladimir Putin who owns the responsibility for energy prices to the extent that they come from that part of the world.”Trump’s decision also garnered international criticism, with the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issuing a statement in support of Ukraine.“This agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” Carney’s office said in a read-out of a call on Sunday with Zelenskyy. “It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine.”

sources.headline: Ukraine says it won't stop attacking Russian oil resources amid diesel fuel deal with U.S.
sources.text:
President Trump is arguing that Ukraine needs a new president as Volodymyr Zelenskyy refuses to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries despite the country's commitment to provide diesel fuel to the U.S. Kamal Afzali has the story.
